title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction: This page completes Euler's count of primitive roots modulo a prime P. On the previous page he proved that if a is a primitive root mod P, with Q = P−1, and gcd(n,Q)=1, then a^n is also a primitive root. The reason is that a^{kn} ≡ 1 exactly when Q divides kn, which forces Q to divide k. Coroll. 1 (§45) gives worked examples. For P=5 (a=2) the primitive roots are 2^1=2 and 2^3≡3. For P=7 (a=3) they are 3^1=3 and 3^5≡5. For P=11 (a=2), using the exponents 1,3,7,9 that are coprime to 10, they are 2, 8, 7, 6. Euler refers back to the complete residue tables of §38. Coroll. 2 (§46) states that the number of primitive roots mod P equals the number of integers below Q=P−1 that are coprime to Q, i.e. φ(P−1). He gives the product formula: if Q=α^λ β^μ γ^ν… then φ(Q) = α^{λ−1}(α−1) β^{μ−1}(β−1)…. Coroll. 3 (§47) gives a sieve: from the numbers below Q, delete those sharing a factor with Q; the rest, always including 1, are coprime to Q. Scholion §48, continued on the next page, begins the converse. If gcd(m,Q)=d>1, then a^{(Q/d)m} = (a^Q)^{m/d} ≡ 1 before the exponent reaches Qm. The residue series of a^m is then incomplete, so a^m is not primitive. Hence there are exactly φ(P−1) primitive roots. All of this serves the paper's broader aim: proving facts about power residues, and the existence and structure of primitive roots, for prime moduli.
errors: No computational errors: 2^3≡3 (mod 5), 3^5≡5 (mod 7), and 2^3≡8, 2^7≡7, 2^9≡6 (mod 11) all check.

Logical caveat, not an error on this page: the count φ(P−1) assumes a primitive root exists. That existence is established elsewhere in E449 by an argument Gauss (Disq. Arith. art. 56) judged incomplete. The 'exactly' part also needs the converse given in §48.

ideas.what: Powers a^n of a primitive root with gcd(n,P−1)=1 are exactly the primitive roots, illustrated mod 5, 7, 11
ideas.modern_name: Generators of the cyclic group (Z/pZ)^* are g^k with gcd(k,p−1)=1

ideas.what: Number of primitive roots mod prime P equals φ(P−1), computed via the prime factorization of P−1
ideas.modern_name: Count of primitive roots = φ(p−1); Euler product formula for the totient

deep.surprise_reason: Well-known content of E449: Euler's count of primitive roots as φ(p−1), with standard examples. It is credited to Euler in Gauss and in standard histories; nothing new.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image; 'a^1 et a^3' (P=5) and 'a^1 et a^5' (P=7) are confirmed. The stray comma in '1, 3, 7, 9' and the subscript-like marks in the image are print artifacts.
